source.title: TYKS regional antimicrobial recommendations
source.authors: Infectious disease physicians at TYKS, Satasairaala and Vaasa Central Hospital, with other specialties (p. 6).
source.translation_status: Selected English translation and summary; not an official or clinically reviewed translation.
source.coverage: Sampling, diagnostic assessment, susceptibility interpretation and antimicrobial stewardship, with selected treatment principles. Full dosing tables and complete treatment regimens are not transcribed.
source.currency: The supplied PDF edition is used; it is not automatically refreshed or verified as the latest publisher version.

scope.population: General hospital antimicrobial guidance for adults; not a pediatric antimicrobial treatment guideline.
scope.organ_function: The source's doses assume normal renal and hepatic function; patient-specific adjustment and interaction checks are separate requirements.
scope.specialist_review: The guide does not replace infectious diseases consultation; it recommends early consultation for immunocompromised patients.
scope.historical_tables: The susceptibility percentages on p. 8 describe TYKS isolates from 2021. The dosing interpretation table cites EUCAST version 11.0 on p. 18. Neither is a current breakpoint table or live hospital antibiogram.
scope.not_covered_here: This English context does not reproduce laboratory SOPs, disk-diffusion/MIC procedures, current numeric breakpoints, full dose schedules or all non-bacterial chapters.

sections.title: Assessment and sampling before antibiotics
facts: Identify the likely infection focus and organisms, distinguishing community-onset from healthcare-associated infection.

Review relevant resistant organisms in risk information and cultures from at least the preceding year, antimicrobials in the preceding 3 months, hospitalization abroad in 12 months, and travel in Asia or Africa in 6 months.
Collect focus-appropriate cultures before starting antibiotics, such as urine, blood or material from the infection site. Sampling must not delay antibiotics in a septic patient.
Check antibiotic allergy history, kidney and liver function, and medication interactions before choosing treatment.

sections.title: Review and target treatment after 48-72 hours
facts: Reassess clinical response, infection focus and culture results within 48-72 hours; aim for the narrowest effective treatment and stop antibiotics if the presumed infection is not present.
Document the treatment indication or working diagnosis, update it as the diagnosis becomes clearer, and record the planned duration.
Clinical response and inflammatory-marker timing matter: CRP may only start falling on treatment day 3-4. A single culture or biomarker does not replace clinical assessment.

sections.title: Interpreting S, I and R
facts: S means susceptible at standard exposure or dosing. I means susceptible with increased exposure, achieved through an appropriately higher or more frequent dose depending on the drug. R means resistant.
I must not be translated as resistant or as the older intermediate category. The source notes some organism-drug combinations are reported only as I or R.

Interpret treatment options using the reported susceptibility, organism, infection site and organ function. The source's dosing table assumes normal renal function and cites EUCAST v11.0; it does not establish today's numeric breakpoints.

sections.title: Historical susceptibility percentages
facts: The spectrum table reports susceptible proportions from TYKS Clinical Microbiology in 2021, intended to help empirical choices when an organism is known but individual susceptibility is pending.

These historical proportions are not a patient's measured result, a model prediction, the dashboard's current synthetic antibiogram or evidence of present-day coverage. Verify a current laboratory standard separately for breakpoint or testing-method questions.

sections.title: Preliminary blood-culture Gram stain
facts: Gram-negative rods can include E. coli, Klebsiella, Pseudomonas, Salmonella and other Enterobacterales; Gram-negative diplococci suggest meningococcus.
Gram-positive cocci may represent streptococci, pneumococci, enterococci or staphylococci depending on morphology. Gram-positive rods can include Listeria and organisms that may be contaminants.

These are preliminary possibilities, not a definitive species identification. Use the final identification and susceptibility as soon as available, alongside the infection focus and source-control assessment.

sections.title: Staphylococcus aureus in blood cultures
facts: S. aureus bloodstream infection requires infectious diseases consultation, follow-up blood cultures until clearance, assessment of the primary focus and deep infection, and echocardiography to exclude endocarditis.

The source distinguishes oxacillin-susceptible S. aureus, for which cloxacillin is listed, from MRSA, for which vancomycin and specialist-selected alternatives are discussed. These are guideline options, not proof of susceptibility in an individual isolate.
Reassess treatment when susceptibility becomes available. Rifampicin and fusidic acid must not be used alone because resistance develops readily.

sections.title: Possible blood-culture contamination
facts: Coagulase-negative staphylococci, Cutibacterium, coryneforms and Bacillus may represent contamination, but coagulase-negative staphylococci may also cause catheter or foreign-body infection.

Interpret the organism with the clinical situation, repeat cultures and device information; do not automatically dismiss the finding. The guide recommends a low threshold for infectious diseases consultation for Gram-positive rod findings.

sections.title: Enterobacterales and inducible resistance
facts: The guide highlights Enterobacter cloacae, Serratia marcescens, Citrobacter freundii and Klebsiella aerogenes as generally cefuroxime resistant, with possible development of ceftriaxone resistance during treatment because of AmpC.

Susceptibility-guided options discussed include cefepime, ertapenem or meropenem, and piperacillin-tazobactam in less severe infections. Clinical severity, infection focus and organ function remain relevant.
A conflict between a recorded result and an expected organism pattern calls for microbiology review; this guidance must not overwrite a measured laboratory result.

sections.title: ESBL, CPE, MRSA and VRE findings
facts: The guide treats ESBL, CPE, MRSA and VRE as clinically and infection-control relevant findings; CPE and VRE require infectious diseases consultation, and MRSA bloodstream infection also requires specialist input.

For systemic ESBL infection, carbapenem options are discussed; meropenem is selected instead of ertapenem when Pseudomonas coverage is needed or albumin is below 25 g/L. This does not make every ESBL-positive urine culture an indication for a carbapenem.
Select treatment from the actual susceptibility and infection context. Resistance to one antibiotic alone does not establish an ESBL, CPE, MRSA or VRE diagnosis.

sections.title: Pseudomonas aeruginosa
facts: The guide recommends infectious diseases consultation and susceptibility-based antipseudomonal treatment. Once susceptibility is known, a single active beta-lactam usually suffices; severe sepsis or neutropenia may require a different initial approach.
Ertapenem does not cover Pseudomonas or enterococci. A carbapenem name or a model ranking is not sufficient evidence of antipseudomonal activity.
Aminoglycoside use requires attention to drug levels and kidney function.

sections.title: Species-specific enterococcal interpretation
facts: The source distinguishes E. faecalis, E. faecium and E. gallinarum. Ampicillin is discussed for susceptible E. faecalis; resistant or allergy situations require alternative assessment.
Vancomycin is not an option for E. gallinarum in this guide. VRE requires susceptibility-guided specialist advice. Persistent fever raises the question of endocarditis.
The historical p. 8 table distinguishes imipenem from meropenem for E. faecalis; these drugs must not be treated as interchangeable.

sections.title: Suspected sepsis and urgent sampling
facts: Sepsis involves infection with organ dysfunction; a positive blood culture is not required. The source discusses bedside deterioration signs and urgent assessment, treatment and source control.
Obtain blood cultures promptly, but do not delay urgent treatment while waiting for other investigations or sampling. Revise empirical therapy as culture results become available.
Empirical choices depend on infection focus, healthcare association, resistance history and immune status. A blood-culture result alone cannot determine whether a patient has sepsis.

sections.title: Fever in a neutropenic patient
facts: Clinical examination and blood cultures precede antimicrobial treatment where possible; additional imaging and microbiological investigations must not delay starting treatment.
Risk assessment considers the depth and expected duration of neutropenia, general condition, prior antimicrobials and resistant-organism carriage. Clinical risk scores require their actual inputs.
The guide separates low- and high-risk pathways and recommends specialist input for severe illness or difficult-to-treat organisms; a ward code is not evidence of neutropenia.

sections.title: Cystitis, pyelonephritis and prostatitis
facts: The guide has separate pathways for uncomplicated female cystitis, pregnancy-associated cystitis or bacteriuria, recurrent infection, pyelonephritis, and male febrile or afebrile infections. A urine isolate does not determine which syndrome is present.

For uncomplicated female cystitis it lists trimethoprim, nitrofurantoin or pivmecillinam; ESBL cystitis options depend on susceptibility and include nitrofurantoin, fosfomycin or higher-exposure pivmecillinam.

Pyelonephritis and febrile male infections need a separate assessment. Nitrofurantoin must not be used when prostatitis is suspected. Final selection is based on susceptibility and the clinical syndrome.
Pregnancy and asymptomatic bacteriuria require their own clinical assessment; pregnancy status and urinary symptoms cannot be assumed from this project's microbiology records.

sections.title: Colonization versus chronic wound infection
facts: Chronic wound surfaces are almost always colonized. Antibiotics are not needed when there is no wound infection; a positive surface culture alone does not establish tissue infection.
Obtain cultures before treatment in moderate or severe infections, and in mild infection when recurrent, after substantial previous antibiotics or with known MRSA carriage.
Assess severity, depth, surrounding inflammation, systemic findings and possible bone or foreign-body involvement. Review recent culture findings and the need for drainage or surgery.

sections.title: Postoperative infection and abscess sampling
facts: Contact the operating unit before starting antibiotics for a suspected surgical wound infection; revision or drainage and microbiological sampling are central.
For suspected prosthetic-joint infection, obtain aspirate or operative cultures before antibiotics unless the patient is septic.
Abscess drainage is often the most important treatment. Obtain pus culture if starting an antibiotic; recurrent abscesses warrant consideration of MRSA and the source's StauPVL test.

sections.title: Necrotizing soft-tissue infection
facts: Rapid surgical assessment and sufficiently extensive debridement are essential; other interventions must not delay necessary surgery.

At revision, obtain tissue for urgent Gram stain and bacterial culture, notify the laboratory of the suspicion, and obtain blood cultures. If antibiotics were already given, also obtain tissue for bacterial nucleic-acid testing.

The source discusses streptococcal, clostridial and mixed infections, with exposure-related organisms after seawater or freshwater injuries. These diagnoses require clinical findings and exposure history.

sections.title: Pneumonia and pleural infection
facts: Different pathways apply to community-onset, hospital-acquired, ICU-level and immunocompromised pneumonia. Review previous sputum isolates and antimicrobials in chronic lung disease.
For immunocompromised pneumonia the source recommends infectious diseases consultation, bronchoscopy and infection-focused bronchoalveolar lavage investigations.
Pleural empyema requires drainage or surgical evaluation and treatment directed by cultures obtained during drainage; drainage is decisive.

sections.title: Bacterial diarrhoea and EHEC
facts: The guide advises considering EHEC in bloody diarrhoea and does not recommend routine antibiotics for EHEC because of the risk of a worse outcome; a septic presentation requires separate urgent clinical management.
Mild or improving Campylobacter infection, mild non-typhoidal Salmonella enteritis and mild Yersinia diarrhoea often do not need antibiotics; severity and patient risk factors change management.
Symptomatic Shigella infection is treated according to susceptibility. An E. coli urinary isolate is not evidence of EHEC or an enteric syndrome.

sections.title: NAAT and culture in bacterial sexually transmitted infection
facts: Gonorrhoea and chlamydia diagnostics use urine or site-appropriate mucosal nucleic-acid testing. If gonococcus is detected by PCR, obtain gonococcal culture for susceptibility testing before treatment.
Indicate suspected LGV on the chlamydia test request so genotyping can be considered. Mycoplasma genitalium resistance testing may be possible on the nucleic-acid-test specimen.
These investigations are described in the guide but their results are not supplied in the project's routine blood, urine and wound culture tables.

sections.title: Suspected endocarditis and cardiac-device infection
facts: Obtain multiple blood cultures before antibiotics where possible. During treatment the guide recommends cultures every 1-2 days until negative and consultation with infectious diseases and cardiology.
Streptococcal endocarditis regimens depend on measured penicillin MIC; request the MIC from the laboratory. S/R data alone do not supply a numeric MIC.

Suspected pacemaker infection requires blood cultures and specialist consultation before empirical antibiotics; purulent drainage and removed device or pocket material require microbiological sampling.

sections.title: Native and prosthetic joint infection
facts: Before antimicrobial treatment obtain blood cultures and a sterile joint-fluid sample for cell count and differential, bacterial culture, Gram stain, bacterial nucleic-acid testing and crystals.

Prosthetic-joint evaluation should involve the prosthetic surgery unit, with aspiration under appropriate sterile operative conditions. If septic, start treatment immediately and obtain samples as quickly as possible.
Interpret negative microbiology alongside clinical suspicion; it does not by itself exclude purulent arthritis. Directed treatment follows susceptibility and specialist review.

sections.title: Diabetic and ischaemic foot infection
facts: Assess clinical severity and obtain bacterial cultures. In mild infection, additional surface isolates may reflect colonization selected by sampling technique or previous antibiotics.

In moderate or severe infection initially consider a mixed infection rather than immediately narrowing to a single isolate. Blood-culture pathogens and deep abscess or operative findings require attention.
Bone sampling can guide osteomyelitis treatment. With a poor response reassess antimicrobial coverage, adequacy of surgery and circulation.

sections.title: Osteomyelitis and spondylodiscitis
facts: Before treatment, seek a representative abscess or infected-bone sample for bacterial culture, nucleic-acid testing and histopathology; consider fungal or mycobacterial studies according to presentation and risk factors.
Obtain blood cultures particularly with fever or systemic illness and assess the need for surgery when an abscess or foreign body is present.

For spondylodiscitis, seek vertebral or abscess samples unless the pathogen is established by blood cultures. In a non-septic patient a clinician may defer treatment briefly to obtain planned samples; this exception must not be extended to a septic patient.

sections.title: Suspected meningitis, brain abscess and shunt infection
facts: Suspected bacterial meningitis is urgent. Where CT is required before lumbar puncture, take blood cultures promptly and start the indicated urgent treatment before waiting for imaging or CSF sampling.
A brain abscess generally requires microbiological sampling unless the cause is already established from blood cultures, with infectious diseases input. Infection site and drug penetration matter.
For shunt infection, review CSF or removed-shunt culture susceptibility and involve neurosurgery and infectious diseases. A routine blood or urine culture is not a CSF investigation.

sections.title: Peritoneal and intra-abdominal infection sampling
facts: PD-associated peritonitis evaluation includes PD-fluid cells and differential, bacterial Gram stain and culture, and a culture from the catheter exit site; additional investigations depend on the case.

Obtain drainage or abscess material for microbiology where possible, with attention to nucleic-acid testing if antibiotics have already started. Suspected liver abscess warrants early specialist advice about appropriate samples.
Infected pancreatic necrosis or peripancreatic abscess calls for image-guided sampling where possible and treatment directed by the results. Source control is a central part of management.

sections.title: Treatment duration and source control
facts: The duration table is indicative, not a universal schedule. Duration depends on response, underlying disease, deep infection and adequacy of surgical source control.

The general duration section does not replace the separate endocarditis guidance. Different passages contain syndrome-specific schedules; do not silently reconcile them into an invented patient regimen.
Culture dates alone do not establish when treatment began or whether blood cultures have cleared. Those dates must not be invented to calculate a stop date.

sections.title: Therapeutic drug and toxicity monitoring
facts: Vancomycin and aminoglycosides need attention to kidney function and drug concentrations. Monitoring depends on the drug, dosing approach and infection; a susceptibility result is not a drug-level measurement.

Long courses require laboratory safety monitoring. The prosthetic-joint section calls for at least weekly blood counts, CRP, electrolytes, creatinine and liver tests, with more frequent renal and drug-level monitoring for nephrotoxic treatment.

This project's microbiology records do not provide therapeutic drug levels, current renal function or actual administered doses. The full source contains concentration targets; they are not transcribed into this summary.

sections.title: Penicillin and beta-lactam allergy assessment
facts: Clarify the implicated drug, when the reaction occurred, timing after exposure, rash characteristics, severity, hospitalization and whether anaphylaxis occurred.

An old allergy label is not a complete assessment. The source describes clinically supervised reassessment for selected low-risk histories, with contraindications including anaphylaxis, serious systemic or severe skin reactions, and clinical instability.
Do not infer absence of allergy from a missing database field, remove an allergy label automatically, or turn this summary into a drug-challenge protocol. Specialist assessment may be needed.

sections.title: Yeast in a blood culture
facts: The guide states that yeast or Candida in blood cultures must not be dismissed as contamination and requires infectious diseases consultation and treatment assessment.
Repeat blood cultures and evaluate catheters, foreign bodies and deep foci. Candida is not a bacterium, and an antibacterial model ranking is not antifungal treatment guidance.
